view: A report says Joseph tested the approaching famine by giving each man two portions; when one ate both, Joseph announced that the hard years had begun.

A report recounts Joseph's famine economy: he stockpiled harvests, exchanged food successively for money, valuables, livestock, servants, property, land and people's freedom, then freed the Egyptians and restored their possessions and kingship.

Whether dreams take effect according to their first interpretation is debated: counselors dismissed the king's dream as confused; al-Alusi responds that such dismissal may not count as interpretation, and Ibn al-ʿArabī restricts the rule to dreams allowing several meanings.
note: Al-Alusi cites the hadith of a dream suspended on a bird's wing until interpreted.

view: Al-Ṣādiq reports a revealed wording 'what you bring near for them' in the preceding passage and explains the following year as one of rain.
The commentator omits other famine-economy reports because most do not directly clarify these verses.

The passage is cited to show that an unbeliever may have a true dream; advice on when to ask for interpretation and a claim that a sleeping dream interprets itself are also transmitted, though al-Alusi finds many such claims opaque.
Joseph guided Egypt through the drought and gained admiration from the king and ordinary people.
Joseph's revealed forecast and the king's dream illustrate that dreams should be interpreted by qualified people.
Unlike a romantic account of Joseph's fortunes, the Qur'anic story illustrates God's hidden direction of human affairs: people may dislike what benefits them or love what harms them.

words: ثُمَّ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ عَامٌۭ
view: Ending Joseph's answer with this glad news comforts people after the discouraging drought forecast and highlights his excellence; his answer to the prisoners placed the prediction first.

words: ثُمَّ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ عَامٌۭ
view: The favorable year follows the seven years of drought, after the earlier seven fertile years; it brings rain, renewed crops and plentiful food.

words: ثُمَّ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ عَامٌۭ
view: Joseph's specific forecast of the additional prosperous year was beyond the king's dream or question and came by divine revelation or knowledge of the unseen; it demonstrates his prophetic knowledge, truthfulness or merit.
note: Some notes say the return of fertility was expected, but only the detailed promise required revelation.

words: ثُمَّ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ عَامٌۭ
view: The dream or God's customary relief after hardship could allow Joseph to infer a fertile year following the drought; the repeated seven likewise suggests the end of strict management of sowing and reserves.
note: Al-Alusi rejects this as too vague to establish the specific forecast; Baydawi allows inference or revelation.

words: ثُمَّ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ عَامٌۭ
view: Joseph's speech offers three elements: interpretation of the dream by meaning, practical advice for the drought, and an announcement of the following year.

words: ثُمَّ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ عَامٌۭ
view: The dream's fat cows and green ears stand for fertile years, lean cows and dry ears for famine, and the swallowing for stored plenty being consumed; the final year is attached as glad tidings after that interpretation.
note: Al-Tabataba'i rejects treating the dream as itself a forecast of the seven fertile and seven barren years and sees Joseph's answer as a survival policy.

words: ثُمَّ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ عَامٌۭ
view: The fruitful year of relief and pressing signifies the soul's enjoyment after complete tranquility and security.
The masculine demonstrative refers to the seven years, since the form sabʿ lacks a feminine marker and can take masculine agreement.
note: Al-Kalbi supports this usage with a parallel verse; Muqatil instead takes the demonstrative to mean the drought.

view: The demonstrative refers to the drought.
note: An alternative refers it to the seven years.

view: ʿĀm denotes a full twelve-month year; compared with sana, it often evokes ease and fertility after the years of hardship.

words: عَامٌۭ فِيهِ يُغَاثُ ٱلنَّاسُ وَفِيهِ يَعْصِرُونَ
view: The year brings ample blessing for people and livestock, with rain or divine aid, crops or fodder, and produce or milk.
The particular full year of abundance and relief follows God's pattern of ease after hardship and brings comfort and hope.
Calling the coming period a year signals that its relief is known and governed by God alone.
Yughāthu means people receive rain; ghayth denotes rain arriving when needed, and its root may be the triliteral ghātha.
note: Some contrast derivation from ghayth (rain) with ghawth (relief); al-Tabataba'i prefers rain because pressing follows.

view: Yughāthu means people are aided or rescued from famine; ghawth is urgent help that removes harm, and this sense may derive from the quadriliteral aghātha.
note: The alternative rain derivation is also reported; Islahi prefers the appeal-for-help sense and calls rain its consequence.

view: Yughāthu can mean people receive abundant produce or vegetation grown by rainwater.
People press crops for juice or oil in the fertile year: grapes, olives, sesame, and, in some accounts, sugarcane, radish, dates or other fruits; the harvest is plentiful again.
note: Several reports specify sesame and olives for oil, grapes for wine or juice, and oil or sweet syrup among usual products.

view: The verb can mean milking livestock, an act of squeezing the udder and a sign of abundant pasture or vegetation.
note: The reading with tāʾ addresses the people as milkers in reports from Ibn Abbas; a poem is cited for the milking usage.

view: ʿAṣr or ʿaṣra can mean rescue, refuge or escape; the people are delivered from drought and distress by the new abundance. Arabic idioms and poems by Labīd, ʿAdī, Abū Zubayd and others support this usage.
note: Al-Tabari rejects the derivation against the early interpreters' consensus; Ibn ʿAtiyya says his rejection lacks proof. Al-Samin prefers rescue because it echoes yughāthu.

view: The verb can mean obtaining what one desires, supported by Ibn Aḥmar's poem about taking from life's branches.
The verb can mean giving generously or granting gifts.
The verb can mean improving and prospering, or receiving plentiful produce, with poetic usage for treating people well.
The verb can refer to bringing livestock in from abundant pasture.
The verb can describe people receiving rain from clouds that release their water; the action may be attributed to the people figuratively or through an omitted preposition.
note: Al-Jawharī gives ʿaṣara al-qawm directly as 'the people received rain,' without supplying an omitted phrase.

view: Pressing may mean extracting produce or wealth for use; iʿtaṣartu mālahu means extracting someone's property from his hand.
In one explanation, the active verb has a consequential sense of abundant rainfall and productive grape vines.

Repeating fīhi separates rain or relief as God's act from pressing as people's act; it can also enumerate benefits, distinguish times or kinds of benefit, emphasize how much greater the rain is than during the drought, or serve the rhyme.
note: Al-Alusi also notes that fronting the phrase marks its focus.

view: Mentioning pressed crops explicitly is special good news because rain does not ensure them as directly as grain; it may also suit the king's circumstances and the second-person reading.
note: Islahi links grape pressing specifically to the king's wine-server.

view: Joseph shifts from direct address to 'people' and third-person pressing, suggesting they will no longer need special management of their livelihoods.

Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read third-person yaʿṣirūn, referring to the people; Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read second-person taʿṣirūn, addressing Joseph's listeners in continuity with his direct speech.
note: Al-Tabari accepts both established readings as equivalent in meaning; some notes identify the addressees specifically as the petitioners.

view: A passive reading yuʿṣarūn, attributed to Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, al-Aʿraj and ʿĪsā, can mean people are rained upon or rescued from hardship.
note: ʿAlī rejects wine pressing and corrects to rain; al-Tabari rejects the reported rain reading because it conflicts with established regional readings. Several cite 78:14.

view: A second-person passive taʿṣarūn attributed to ʿĪsā means the listeners are rescued from hardship or rained upon.
note: Al-Qurtubi also records a kasra on the ṣād with the rain meaning.

view: Al-Naqqāsh records an intensive reading with a doubled ṣād, conveying intensity or abundance and allowing pressing, milking or rescue.
Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads an assimilated form of taʿtaṣirūn; it can mean squeezing produce or being delivered.
note: The descriptions differ on whether the assimilated form is written taʿtaṣirūn or taʿaṣṣarūn.

view: A reading attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās uses second-person taʿṣirūn with the sense that the listeners milk animals.
Al-Tabari rejects a reported reading meaning 'they are rained upon' because it differs from the established regional readings.
note: Other sources transmit and explain this passive rain reading.

view: The people cry to God in the extreme drought, and their pleas are answered with rain and aid.
Egyptian agriculture can still be described as receiving rain because rain upstream in Sudan feeds the Nile floods on which Egyptian crops depend.
note: Al-Tabataba'i rejects the objection that Egypt relies on Nile flooding rather than local rain.

view: The rain sense fits the next clause about pressing produce better than the general sense of aid.
note: Al-Tabataba'i allows aid to fit better if the following verb is read passively as being rained upon.

view: Pressing produce visibly marks the transition to prosperity: during the famine people pressed nothing, according to one report, or had gone fourteen years without pressing oil or grapes.

Al-Tabari rejects deriving the active verb from rescue because the Companions and Successors unanimously interpreted it as pressing produce; he also rejects a report through al-Faraj ibn Faḍāla from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa as contrary to known Arabic and Ibn ʿAbbās's usage.
note: Ibn ʿAtiyya says al-Tabari supplies no proof against the rescue derivation.

view: The passive rain reading is preferred in reports from ʿAlī and al-Ṣādiq: it describes rain falling on people, as with the rain clouds of 78:14, rather than pressing wine.
Severe hardship drives even polytheists and disbelievers to call on the one God and forget their imagined deities.
